#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP)
Description: The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), also known as The Nation's Report Card, is the largest ongoing, nationally representative assessment of education in the United States. Since 1969, NAEP has served as a vital measure of student achievement, providing valuable insights into academic performance and learning experiences across various subjects. Its results offer a comprehensive view of educational progress at the national level, across states, and in 27 urban districts.
URL: https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP)
Description: The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), also known as The Nation's Report Card, is the largest ongoing, nationally representative assessment of education in the United States. Since 1969, NAEP has served as a vital measure of student achievement, providing valuable insights into academic performance and learning experiences across various subjects. Its results offer a comprehensive view of educational progress at the national level, across states, and in 27 urban districts.
URL: https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the NAEP dataset from multiple angles. Let me start with several parallel searches.I have good coverage of basics, authority, users, and recent news. Now let me dig into data access details, methodology, and preservation concerns.I've hit the search result limit, but I have substantial material. Let me fetch a couple of key pages directly to fill remaining gaps on the 2025 cutbacks and preservation concerns.I now have comprehensive material from official sources (NCES, NAGB, U.S. Code, CRS), news coverage, and the program's own technical documentation. Here is the complete report.

---

# Research Report: The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP)

## 1. Verification of the Provided Description

The description you provided is **accurate and consistent with official sources**, with minor notes:

- ✅ "The Nation's Report Card" is the correct public brand name.
- ✅ NAEP is indeed the largest ongoing, nationally representative assessment of U.S. student achievement; it has operated **since 1969**.
- ✅ Results are reported at the **national level, for states/jurisdictions, and for participating large urban districts**.
- ⚠️ The "27 urban districts" figure is accurate **as of 2017** (per the National Assessment Governing Board), though the roster of Trial Urban District Assessment (TUDA) districts has shifted slightly between administrations.
- ⚠️ Note there are **two related URLs**: the program's hub at `nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard` (technical, participation, and researcher resources) and the results-delivery site `nationsreportcard.gov` (report cards, data tools). Both are official.

---

## 2. Identity and Publisher

**Publisher / operator:**
- **National Center for Education Statistics (NCES)**, the primary federal statistical agency for education, led by the Commissioner of Education Statistics.
- NCES sits within the **Institute of Education Sciences (IES)**, the research arm of the **U.S. Department of Education**.
- NCES carries out the operational components: sampling, administration, scoring, scaling, analysis, and dissemination, largely **through grants, contracts, or cooperative agreements with qualified organizations** (Educational Testing Service was the long-standing prime assessment contractor; vendor arrangements have evolved over time).

**Policy-setting body:**
- The **National Assessment Governing Board (NAGB)** — an independent, bipartisan board of governors, state legislators, state school superintendents, teachers, researchers, and members of the public — **sets policy for NAEP**: it determines assessment content and design, adopts the subject **frameworks**, sets the **assessment schedule**, approves **achievement levels**, and oversees reporting, release of data/items, and evaluation. Board members are appointed by the Secretary of Education; the IES Director serves ex officio (nonvoting).
- The Governing Board and NAEP operations have **separate line items in the federal budget** (through IES's annual appropriation).

**Web presence:**
- Program hub: `https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard` (About, participation, technical documentation, researcher center)
- Results site: `https://www.nationsreportcard.gov` (interactive report cards, NAEP Data Explorer, question tools, profiles)

---

## 3. Legal Authority and Mandate

### Statutory foundation
- NAEP's modern authority is the **National Assessment of Educational Progress Authorization Act** ("NAEPAA"), Title III, Sections 302–303 of **P.L. 107-279** (the Education Sciences Reform Act of 2002), codified at **20 U.S.C. §§ 9621–9622**.
- Section 303 requires the **Commissioner for Education Statistics**, with the advice of NAGB, to carry out a National Assessment consisting of a **national assessment, state assessments, and a long-term trend assessment in reading and mathematics**.
- Stated purpose: *"to provide, in a timely manner, a fair and accurate measurement of student academic achievement and reporting of trends in such achievement."*

### State participation mandate
- Under the **No Child Left Behind Act of 2001** and continued under the **Every Student Succeeds Act of 2015 (ESSA)**, states receiving **Title I funding must participate** in NAEP **reading and mathematics at grades 4 and 8 every two years**. Participation in all other subjects and grades is voluntary.
- The 2001 reauthorization also shifted NAEP's design: from 2002, an **aggregate of all state samples replaced the separate national sample** for main NAEP.

### Key statutory prohibitions (20 U.S.C. § 9622(b)(4)) — critical for understanding NAEP's data design
The law **prohibits** the federal government from using NAEP items or data to:
- **Rank, compare, or evaluate individual students or teachers**, or provide rewards/sanctions for individual students, teachers, schools, or districts;
- **Establish, require, or influence** state/local standards, assessments, curriculum, textbooks, or instructional practices;
- Prescribe NAEP's use for **student promotion or graduation** decisions.

These prohibitions explain why NAEP reports only **group-level results**, tests a **sample** of students, uses **matrix sampling** (each student takes only part of the assessment), and is often described as "low-stakes." Related Education Sciences Reform Act provisions also bar creation of a nationwide database of individually identifiable information.

---

## 4. History and Evolution

| Period | Milestone |
|---|---|
| Early 1960s | U.S. Commissioner of Education **Francis Keppel** champions the first national assessment of student "output" (learning) rather than just "input" statistics (enrollment, spending, etc.) |
| **1969** | First NAEP administration |
| 1969–present | **Long-Term Trend (LTT) assessment** tracks reading and math for ages 9, 13, and 17 using a largely stable design back to the early 1970s |
| 1988 | Congress creates the **National Assessment Governing Board** (via Hawkins-Stafford amendments), separating policy-setting from operations |
| **1990** | First **trial state-level assessments** (voluntary); states join in 1992, authorized as fully operational in 1996 |
| 1990s | **Achievement levels** (Basic, Proficient, Advanced) introduced as reporting benchmarks set by NAGB |
| 1996–2002 | Gradual adoption of **testing accommodations** for students with disabilities and English learners; by 2002 all assessed samples were accommodated and NAEP no longer reported separate non-accommodated samples |
| **2001–2002** | NCLB mandates biennial state participation in grade 4/8 reading and math; all states participate from 2002; aggregate of state samples becomes the national sample |
| **2002** | **Trial Urban District Assessment (TUDA)** launches; grows to **27 voluntary districts as of 2017** (Atlanta, DC, NYC, Los Angeles, Houston, etc.) |
| 2009–2017 | Migration to **computer-based delivery**: computerized interactive science tasks (2009), fully computer-based writing (2011), transition of main assessments to tablets by 2017 |
| **2024** | First administrations using **school internet** and **NAEP-provided Chromebooks** (alongside Surface Pro tablets); a **bridge study** ensured score comparability across devices (lengthening the release timeline by ~3 months) |
| **2025** | Modernization **field test**; **full modernization implemented in 2026** (assessing on familiar school devices, flexible environments, including remote capability) |
| **2025** | Long-Term Trend results for ages 9 and 13 released (9-year-olds' scores rose 4 points in both reading and math vs. 2022) |

---

## 5. What the Dataset Consists Of

### Assessment structure
- **Grades 4, 8, and 12** (main NAEP); **ages 9, 13, 17** (long-term trend).
- **Subjects assessed periodically**: mathematics, reading, science, writing, civics, U.S. history, and technology & engineering literacy (TEL); formerly the arts, economics, and geography. Not every subject is given in every grade or year.
- **Reporting geographies**: nation (public + private), 50 states + DC + DoD schools + (in math) Puerto Rico (53 jurisdictions), and TUDA districts.

### Sample design (a nationally representative probability sample)
- Multistage stratified sampling: schools within strata → students within schools → allocation of students to subjects.
- State samples average **~2,500 students in ~100 public schools per grade, per subject**; typically **~30 students per school per subject**.
- Private school samples are drawn for national estimates.
- Results are **weighted** (inverse of selection probability, adjusted for school/student nonresponse) to be representative of the target populations.

### Psychometrics — important for data scientists
- Items are scored with **Item Response Theory (IRT)**; group score distributions are estimated via **marginal maximum likelihood** latent regression models.
- NAEP uses **matrix sampling**, so no student takes the full assessment; consequently, NAEP produces **plausible values** rather than individual scores. **Twenty plausible values** (draws from each student's predictive conditional distribution) are saved in the data files for secondary analysts, and proper analysis requires using all of them (with jackknife replicate weights for standard errors).
- Results reported as **average scale scores** (0–500 for most subjects; 0–300 for LTT) and as percentages at or above **NAEP Basic, NAEP Proficient, and NAEP Advanced** achievement levels.

### Contextual data
- Students, teachers, and school administrators complete **survey questionnaires** about educational experiences, providing context (course-taking, instructional practices, school climate, etc.).
- **Linked and special studies**: High School Transcript Study (HSTS), National Indian Education Study (NIES), Monthly School Survey (during COVID), **process data** (log-file/clickstream data from computer-based assessments), state proficiency mapping studies, NAEP–TIMSS linking studies, and Puerto Rico mathematics studies.

---

## 6. Data Products and Access (for librarians and data scientists)

**Public tools (no license required):**
- **NAEP Data Explorer (NDE)** — web-based tool for building statistical tables, charts, and maps from most NAEP data **from 1990 to date**, including special versions for LTT, HSTS, and NIES. Requires agreeing to NCES data-usage terms.
- **NAEP Questions Tool (NQT)** — browse released assessment items.
- **State and District Profiles**, performance snapshots, school-type dashboards, item maps.
- **NAEP API** (documented at nationsreportcard.gov) for programmatic access to results.
- Variable listings for each assessment year downloadable in Excel/CSV without a license.

**Restricted-use microdata (license required):**
- Respondent-level data (including weights and plausible values) on **CD-ROM, from the 1990 assessment onward**.
- Access requires an organizational **restricted-use data license** from NCES, applied for via the federal **Standard Application Process (SAP) Portal** (sap.nsf.gov, used since December 2022). Licenses impose security plans, data-safeguarding obligations, and compliance inspections; loans are to qualified U.S. organizations only, with a designated Principal Project Officer.

**Analysis software:**
- **EdSurvey** (free R package from AIR/NCES), **AM Statistical Software**, and the **NAEP Data Toolkit** — all built to handle NAEP's plausible values, weights, and complex sample design.

**Documentation:**
- Extensive **technical documentation** (the "TDW") covering sampling, weighting, scaling, analysis, and data codes, plus the NCES Handbook of Survey Methods chapter and a periodic **NAEP Data Dictionary/compendium**. NAEP results also feed the **Digest of Education Statistics**.

---

## 7. Typical Users and Uses

- **Federal policymakers and Congress**: NAEP is the only common national yardstick of achievement; the program is congressionally mandated precisely to monitor national outcomes of education.
- **State leaders**: NAEP is the **only assessment permitting valid comparisons across all 53 states/jurisdictions**. States use it to (1) validate and track their own standards and assessments over time (state tests change frequently; NAEP is constant), (2) benchmark against peer states, (3) catalyze policy change (e.g., Colorado's math tutoring investments and Florida's reading legislation after NAEP declines), and (4) increase transparency. The National Governors Association has used NAEP to orient incoming governors.
- **Researchers**: A foundational dataset for education research. Sean Reardon (Stanford) and colleagues combine NAEP with state test data to build common cross-district scales for equity research; NAEP's disaggregation by race/ethnicity, gender, disability status, English-learner status, and lunch eligibility underpins much of the achievement-gap literature.
- **Advocates and think tanks**: The Education Trust, UnidosUS, AEI, and others use NAEP to document inequities and argue for policy responses ("Distance to 100," learning-recovery funding, reading-science reforms).
- **Media**: Each release generates major national coverage (AP, NPR, EdWeek, etc.).
- **Educators**: Use frameworks, released items ("Take NAEP Now," sample question booklets), item maps, and achievement-level descriptions in the classroom.
- **Parents and the public**: State/district report cards and profiles make performance transparent in plain language.

### Benefits to the public
- **A common, consistent measure** of what American students know and can do — independent of differing state standards and tests, which vary in rigor and scale.
- **Trend measurement spanning 50+ years** (LTT back to the early 1970s), enabling detection of long-run changes such as the pandemic-era declines and the partial 2025 recovery among 9-year-olds.
- **Equity transparency**: disaggregated results by student group, urban districts, and more — data advocates call it "a level of transparency to an otherwise opaque education system."
- **Low-stakes, privacy-protective design**: no individual student, teacher, or school results; by law it cannot be used for sanctions or to dictate curriculum.
- **Free public access** to results, tools, and (with license) microdata.

---

## 8. Limitations and Criticisms (context for analysts)

- NAEP **cannot support causal inference** from its cross-sectional correlations; NCES itself cautions against interpreting relationships between background variables and scores as causal.
- Group-level design means **no individual scores**; plausible values, matrix sampling, and jackknife weights require specialized analysis (misuse by naïve analysts is a known problem).
- **Framework revisions and design changes** (e.g., new reading frameworks, the 2024 device transition, accommodation policy changes pre-2002) create comparability breaks; analysts must consult trend-bridge documentation.
- Periodic criticism of achievement-level setting (e.g., debates over whether "Proficient" is too stringent a bar).
- Sample sizes at district/state-by-subject-by-grade levels limit precision for small subgroups.

---

## 9. Preservation, Governance, and Risk Considerations (2024–2026)

This is a fast-moving area that preservationists should track closely:

- **March 2025**: The Trump administration cut nearly the entire staff of NCES (and over half of IES staff) as part of broad Education Department reductions — raising serious concerns about the program's operational and statistical capacity.
- **April 2025**: NAGB announced that NAEP will **shrink in scope through 2032**: the 2028 4th-grade science assessment is cancelled; 12th graders will not be assessed in science or U.S. history through 2032 (only 8th grade history remains in 2030); the 2032 writing assessment was cancelled for all grades; state-level results won't be produced for 12th-grade reading/math in the next two administrations, nor for the 2030 8th-grade U.S. history test; district results won't be provided for 8th-grade science. These cuts create **trend-line discontinuities** that researchers will need to document.
- **2025 releases proceeded**: 2024 grades 4/8 math & reading (released January 29, 2025 — further reading declines, a 2-point 4th-grade math gain); 2024 grade-8 science and grade-12 math/reading (September 9, 2025 — declines vs. 2019); 2025 LTT for ages 9 and 13 (recovery among 9-year-olds vs. 2022).
- **Preservation-relevant notes**: NAEP's historical archive depends on federal stewardship (NCES/IES) plus licensed CD-ROM copies held by universities; public results and API endpoints could be vulnerable to website changes under reorganization. The **restricted-use licensing regime** means that raw microdata exist in distributed institutional copies rather than a single public repository — a fact both protective (privacy) and risky (single-copy loss). Data librarians may wish to ensure institutional holdings of restricted-use NAEP CDs, technical documentation, and report-card PDFs are inventoried and redundantly preserved; the **NAEP API** and **Data Explorer** outputs should be harvested periodically.
- The statutory mandate itself (P.L. 107-279; ESSA) has not been repealed, so the program's legal foundation remains, but appropriations, staffing, and schedule decisions determine actual output.

---

## 10. Key Sources Consulted

1. NCES, "About NAEP" — https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/about/
2. NCES, "History and Innovation" — https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/about/naephistory.aspx
3. NAGB, "About NAEP" — https://www.nagb.gov/naep/about-naep.html
4. NAGB, "The NAEP Law" — https://www.nagb.gov/naep/the-naep-law.html (text of 20 U.S.C. §§ 9621–9622; also at https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/20/9622)
5. CRS Report R45401, *National and International Educational Assessments* (2018)
6. NCES Handbook of Survey Methods — NAEP chapters (sample design; uses of data)
7. NCES, NAEP Researchers pages — data availability, restricted-use licensing, software; https://nces.ed.gov/statprog/instruct.asp
8. NAEP Technical Documentation — plausible values methodology — https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/tdw/analysis/est_pv.aspx
9. NAGB, "How States Use and Value NAEP" and "Leveraging NAEP Data to Study and Improve Educational Equity"
10. NAGB news releases: 2024 grades 4/8 results (Jan. 29, 2025); grades 8/12 science, math, reading (Sept. 9, 2025)
11. NAEP 2025 Modernizations FAQ (NCES)
12. Education Week, "Fewer Subjects, Students, Students, Data Points: Feds to Scale Back NAEP" (Apr. 21, 2025); NPR coverage of the Sept. 2025 release
13. NAEP 2025 Long-Term Trend results — https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/ltt/2025/
14. Digest of Education Statistics, Appendix A.2 (NAEP)

---

### Bottom line

NAEP is a **congressionally mandated, federally operated, 55+-year-running national assessment program** published by NCES (within IES/ED) under the NAEP Authorization Act (P.L. 107-279; 20 U.S.C. §§ 9621–22), with policy set by the independent NAGB, and state participation in grade 4/8 reading/math required biennially under ESEA/ESSA as a Title I condition. It is the **only common, cross-state, trend-consistent measure of U.S. student achievement**, used by everyone from Congress and governors to researchers, advocates, journalists, and parents, and it is deliberately designed (sampling, plausible values, statutory prohibitions) to be a low-stakes, privacy-protective group-level indicator. Its data are freely explorable online (NDE, API) and available at the respondent level through a restricted-use license regime dating to 1990. The program's description you supplied is accurate — but anyone preserving or depending on this dataset should be aware of the significant **2025 cutbacks and schedule reductions** that threaten trend continuity through 2032.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- The NAEP Data Explorer (NDE) continues to advertise and provide results from 1990 to present, with special versions for the Long-Term Trend assessment (math since 1978, reading since 1971), the High School Transcript Study, and the National Indian Education Study (nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/researchcenter/datatools.aspx; nationsreportcard.gov/ndecore/help).
- Pre-1990 data (1970–1980 assessments, 1987 HSTS) remain available via ICPSR at the University of Michigan — an off-platform redundancy that predates the current disruption.
- The NAEP Data Service API and restricted-use data (CD-ROM, 1990 onward) infrastructure remain documented as available.
- The NAGB website (nagb.gov) remains live and fully operational (verified October 2026), including historical results pages, the "2024 Nation's Report Card," and interactive trend tools.
- No source in my research — including the ASA's critical "Nation's Data at Risk" profile of NCES, which meticulously catalogs cancellations and delays — reports any removal of *historical* NAEP data files. The documented casualties at NCES (Condition of Education restructuring, Digest table reductions, pulled School Crime report) are other programs' publications, not NAEP's historical archive.

**Evidence for higher levels:** None found. The only caution is structural: NAEP's public archive depends on a hollowed-out agency (see Staffing), and the ASA notes NCES "does not maintain a publication schedule," but no actual removals of prior NAEP data are documented.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** All historical NAEP data appear to remain publicly accessible with no known alterations. (Persistent archival risk exists given agency capacity, but the rubric asks about known removals.)

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- **Skipped collection (mandated component):** The 2024–25 Long-Term Trend age-17 assessment was canceled in February 2025, with ED citing funding issues (Higher Ed Dive; ASA). This is a statutorily required LTT cohort — age 17 LTT has now been skipped since 2012.
- **Skipped collection (voluntary components):** On April 21, 2025, NAGB voted to cancel roughly a dozen assessments through 2032: the 2029 LTT entirely; grade-4 science (2028); grade-12 science (2032); grade-12 U.S. history (2030); writing for all grades (2032); plus dropped state-level results for grade-12 reading/math (2028, 2032) and district-level results for grade-8 science (NAGB news release 4/21/2025; Education Week 4/21/2025; Hechinger Report).
- **Delayed publication:** The 2024 grade-8 science and grade-12 math/reading results, expected summer 2025, were delayed to September 9, 2025 (APM Reports; ASA).
- **Schedule instability:** NAGB passed a resolution asking Congress to move the 2028 assessments to 2029 (nagb.gov, 2025).

**Evidence against "Gone" / mitigating:**
- The legislatively mandated core continues: the 2026 NAEP (grades 4/8 reading and math, grade-8 civics and U.S. history) proceeded under an active ICR.
- **ICR is active and current:** OMB Control No. 1850-0928, "NAEP 2026 Amendment 1," was approved without change September 5, 2025, with expiration 09/30/2028 (reginfo.gov). Amendment 2 was noticed October 2, 2025 (90 FR 47746), and the NAEP 2027 ICR cycle began with a 60-day notice December 18, 2025 (Federal Register), with further revision filings in March and July 2026 (omb.report).
- Data collection and publication have not been terminated.

**Finding: High Risk.** Collection and publication of multiple components have been skipped or cancelled through 2032 (including one statutorily defined LTT cohort), and publication dates have been missed — squarely meeting the "High Risk" definition. It falls short of "Gone" because the congressionally mandated assessments continue with an active, timely-renewed ICR.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- **Granularity reductions:** State-level results eliminated for grade-12 reading/math (2028, 2032) and grade-8 U.S. history (2030); TUDA district-level results eliminated for grade-8 science (2028, 2032) (NAGB 4/21/2025; Education Week).
- **Frequency reductions:** The 2029 LTT administration cancelled outright, breaking a trend line dating to the 1970s; ~a dozen assessments cut from the 2028–2032 schedule; the age-17 LTT gap extends to 20+ years.
- **Timeliness:** 2024 results released ~3 months late (Sept. 2025); NAGB seeks to push the 2028 cycle to 2029.
- **Content reductions:** The 2026 ICR Amendment 1 removed the field trial and dropped pilot teacher and school administrator questionnaires for grade 8 (mainland and Puerto Rico), cutting federal costs by $8.2M (reginfo.gov ICR 202507-1850-004) — fewer contextual data elements collected.
- **Methodological/quality concerns:** All but one NCES psychometrician were laid off; NAGB had to lend five technical staff to NCES; researchers (Sean Reardon, Andrew Ho, Mark Seidenberg) publicly warn that quality and reliability will slip (APM Reports, 8/21/2025). The device/platform modernization (2024–2026) adds comparability strain during a period of minimal oversight capacity.

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":** None. Core mandated assessments (grades 4/8 reading/math) maintained their design and biennial frequency.

**Finding: High Risk.** Documented reductions in granularity (dropped state/district reporting), frequency (cancelled administrations), and timeliness (delayed releases), plus severe degradation of the expert staff who assure quality — well past the "potential or emerging" threshold of Moderate Risk, though not terminated.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- NAEP is explicitly required by the **National Assessment of Educational Progress Authorization Act (P.L. 107-279, Title III, §303)**, codified at 20 U.S.C. §§ 9621–9622, which mandates a national assessment, state assessments, and a long-term trend assessment in reading and mathematics, with prescriptive requirements on what is collected (results disaggregated by race/ethnicity, sex, socioeconomic status, disability, and English proficiency) (NAGB "The NAEP Law"; Federal Register ICR abstract).
- State participation in grades 4/8 reading/math is **required biennially as a condition of Title I funding** under ESSA — making NAEP required for implementation of a federal program.
- **No substitute exists:** NAEP is the only nationally representative, cross-state-comparable measure of student achievement; state tests use differing standards and scales and cannot be aggregated. The CRS, NAGB, and researchers uniformly identify it as unique. Statutory authorization is explicit, not vague.
- The Federal Register ICR abstract (Oct. 2025) itself recites the statutory mandate verbatim.

**Evidence for higher levels:** The March 20, 2025 Executive Order 14242 directing closure of the Department of Education creates uncertainty about the future institutional home of NCES/NAEP, but does not (and cannot, unilaterally) repeal the statutory mandate. Courts have noted the EO directs action only "to the maximum extent appropriate and permitted by law."

**Finding: No Known Issue.** Statutorily required with explicitly named authorization, clear collection requirements, federal-program implementation role (Title I/ESSA), and no alternative data collection that could serve as a substitute. The institutional-relocation question is a staffing/policy matter, not a statutory one.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for "High Risk" (and arguably near "Gone"):**
- **Staff losses far beyond the 40% threshold:** NCES fell from ~102 employees in January 2025 to effectively 3–5 by March 2025 — a ~97% loss (ASA "Nation's Data at Risk"; Inside Higher Ed 3/14/2025; NEPM 3/21/2025). IES overall lost at least 62% of staff (167 → ~62) (Education Week, March 2025); over 1,300 ED employees were terminated overall (NARST et al. joint letter, 3/25/2025).
- **Leadership removed:** Commissioner Peggy Carr (presidentially appointed, six-year term designed for political insulation) was placed on administrative leave February 24, 2025, and later dismissed; the agency operated without a commissioner until Matthew Soldner was named *acting* commissioner July 7, 2025 (ASA; Hechinger interview with Carr).
- **Funding/contracts:** ~$900 million in IES contracts (about three-quarters) were terminated in February 2025, including NAEP operational contracts; DOGE demanded 50% cuts to NAEP contracts, with Carr negotiating a 28% reduction before her removal (Hechinger Report; Inside Higher Ed 2/12/2025). Many contracts were later restored, but the ASA reports that "the extent and revised scope of the contracts are not publicly available."

**Mitigating evidence (against "Gone"):**
- Some restoration occurred: contracts revived, NAGB lent five technical staff, NCES advertised for assessment experts in September 2025 and "added a few staff" in 2026 (ASA "Vision and Strategy for Remaking NCES," summer 2026). The program continues to operate and the 2026 assessment cycle proceeded.
- NAEP and NAGB have separate budget line items; NAGB remains functional and is actively recruiting new board members (verified October 2026).

**Finding: High Risk.** All three High Risk triggers are met (staff loss ≥40% — in fact ~97% at NCES; ≥1,000 staff lost department-wide; leadership removed), compounded by massive contract termination. Not "Gone" because the program retains skeletal staffing, partial contract restoration, ongoing hiring, and a functioning governing board.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- **Executive Order 14242 (March 20, 2025)** directs the Secretary to "facilitate the closure of the Department of Education" — the parent department of NCES/IES. Notably, the EO *cites NAEP results* ("70 percent of 8th graders were below proficient in reading") as justification for closing the department that produces NAEP.
- **Administration-driven changes to what is collected:** NAGB explicitly stated its April 2025 scope reductions responded to "the U.S. Department of Education's stated need to find efficiencies in all Departmental activities, including NAEP" — i.e., the ~dozen cancelled assessments, dropped state/district reporting, and 2029 LTT cancellation are significant changes made in accordance with Administration (DOGE) priorities (NAGB news release; Hechinger: cuts made "to appease Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency").
- **The February 2025 IES contract terminations** (~$900M) were DOGE-driven and directly hit NAEP operations.
- **"Reimagining IES" report (Feb. 2026)**, prepared by senior advisor Dr. Amber Northern, recommends content reviews "to reduce the size of its data collection portfolio" — a formal administration policy document signaling further shrinkage (ies.ed.gov; ASA).
- **Litigation:** Education advocacy groups filed two APA suits over the dismantling of IES; a federal judge denied a preliminary injunction, opining that the APA could not comprehensively undo "multifaceted agency transformations wrought by political decisions" (D.D.C., 2025).

**Evidence for "Moderate" only:** Some actions were proposals/pending (the 2028→2029 shift requires Congress; the IES reorganization report is advisory), and ED publicly defends NAEP's "gold-standard status."

**Evidence against "Gone":** Collection and publication continue; the mandated core assessments were preserved; the administration repeatedly stated NAEP is being maintained.

**Finding: High Risk.** The changes to NAEP's scope were Presidential-action- and administration-priority-driven (EO 14242, DOGE cuts), and are significant, concrete, and already implemented — not merely proposed. This is not "Gone" because the data collection itself survives.

---

## Summary of Risk Levels

| Category | Risk Level | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical Data Availability** | **No Known Issue** | All NAEP data 1971/1990–present remain accessible via NDE, API, ICPSR; no documented removals |
| **Future Data Availability** | **High Risk** | Multiple collections skipped/cancelled through 2032 (incl. age-17 LTT, 2029 LTT, writing, grade-4 science); releases delayed; but mandated core and ICR (1850-0928, exp. 9/30/2028) remain active |
| **Data Quality** | **High Risk** | Documented reductions in granularity (dropped state/district results), frequency (cancelled administrations), and timeliness (delayed releases), plus loss of nearly all psychometric staff |
| **Statutory Context** | **No Known Issue** | Explicitly required by P.L. 107-279 / 20 U.S.C. §§ 9621–22 and ESSA Title I; no alternative data collection can substitute |
| **Staffing and Funding** | **High Risk** | ~97% of NCES staff terminated; ~$900M in contracts cut; commissioner removed; only partial restoration since |
| **Policy** | **High Risk** | EO 14242 to close parent department; DOGE-driven cuts caused NAGB's assessment cancellations; Feb. 2026 IES reorganization report signals further portfolio reduction |

**Overall assessment:** NAEP's historical archive is currently intact and its statutory foundation is unambiguous, but the program is operating under severe, administration-driven stress. The core mandated assessments (grades 4/8 reading/math, LTT ages 9/13) continue with an active ICR, while a large fraction of the voluntary portfolio, several state/district reporting levels, and one statutorily defined cohort (age-17 LTT) have already been sacrificed, and the near-total loss of NCES's technical staff poses an ongoing, unresolved threat to the quality and continuity of future collections.
